extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (early modern philosophy, Hobbes, emotion theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and analyze Thomas Hobbes's account of the passions/emotions: his materialist psychology, classification of passions, felicity, the passion for glory, the relation of passions to reason, and their social-political consequences. The page is a Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry surveying Hobbes's views and influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions as material motions internal to the body
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes identifies passions with material locomotion (motions) internal to the body rather than merely metaphorical motions; they stand between involuntary 'vital' motion and voluntary animal motion and are the interior beginnings of motion (conatus/endeavour) that lead to will and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explains links from external impacts on sense organs to imagination to small beginnings of animal motion (endeavour/conatus) and then deliberation and will. Hobbes sometimes invokes circulation of the blood and animal spirits to explain how changes in vital motion produce appetitive or aversive action, but he does not give detailed physiology of particular passions. The account consistently treats passions as bodily motions sufficient to ground his materialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness (felicity) defined as continual success in satisfying future desires
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness or 'felicity' is described as continual success in satisfying desires in the future (rather than the satisfaction itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes's definition is future-directed and shapes his broader psychological and political theory (e.g., law of nature directing forward-looking preservation of life). The idea connects to the pursuit of power as the means to secure continued success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of definitions and taxonomy for the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes emphasizes definitions and taxonomy: he produces lists of passions, arranges many as contraries, and often treats passions as compounds of simpler elements rather than as a single top-down taxonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Elements of Law's list arranged in contraries; Leviathan's set of six 'simple' passions (with appetite and aversion primary and 'contempt' as a neutral middle), which can be compounded to yield many passions. The entry cites Hobbes's figurative 'footrace' list and notes textual variations across works and over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between sensual pleasures and passions of the mind (temporality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes distinguishes sensual pleasures (directed at present objects) from passions of the mind (concerned with future objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements of Law frames the difference temporally (present vs. future); Leviathan frames it in terms of considering objects as effect, means, or promise. In both accounts Hobbes is chiefly interested in passions concerning objects not yet attained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power as basis for prospect of success and the passion for glory
rubrics_metrics.description: The prospect of success in satisfying passions depends on power; the pursuit of happiness is therefore a striving for power. The passion for 'glory' involves feeling one's own power, desiring recognition, and the eclipse of others' power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glory is a prominent passion in Elements of Law and figures as a cause of conflict in Leviathan. It can motivate self-destructive conquest beyond security needs; it is not universal (some are 'moderate'). Sovereign institutions can channel the passion for glory into socially acceptable forms of recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions in the state of nature and the problem of the 'common measure'
rubrics_metrics.description: In the state of nature, passions such as diffidence and glory, combined with equality of hope and scarcity, generate competition and conflict. Hobbes identifies the lack of a 'common measure'—each person using private passions as the measure of good and evil—as central to the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing a sovereign authority provides a common measure and enforcement, transforms or modifies passions by providing new objects for hopes and fears, and channels competitive drives into cooperative arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions and reason: opposition, interdependence, and motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes often opposes passions to reason (the 'common measure'), but also treats passions as indispensable to life and reasoning: deliberation is an alternation of passions, passions are the 'beginnings of speech' and the material of reasoning, and 'the desires and other passions of man are in themselves no sin.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical problem: reason divorced from passions cannot motivate action. Hobbes holds passions can only be bridled by other passions (not pure reason), especially by the passion of fear. The entry suggests Hobbes may be distinguishing between chaotic/unbridled passions and those channeled by an overriding organizing passion (fear of coercive power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions as motivational (attractive/aversive) and coinciding with the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions have motivating power through their attractive or aversive directions and coincide with the will: interior beginnings of motion in imagination lead to will which produces voluntary motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account connects imagination-caused small motions (endeavour) to deliberation and will. Passions thus function as the proximate movers of action in Hobbes's psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions can be compounds, moods, and character traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes's catalog of passions ranges from ephemeral states (e.g., 'sudden glory' causing laughter), to moods (confidence, diffidence), to durable character traits and dispositions (good nature, covetousness, impudence); many passions are compounds of simpler passions like joy and grief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lists in Elements of Law and Leviathan illustrate this variety and the compositional nature of passions—Hobbes's nets are 'wide' so the term covers many psychological phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defects and disorders of passions
rubrics_metrics.description: An excess of passion may produce giddiness or madness; a 'defect' of passion engenders 'dulnesse'; disorders of passions produce melancholy or enthusiasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes treats degrees and disorders of passion as having psychological consequences (Leviathan 8.16–20); moderation is not simply praised as in Aristotelian frameworks because greater passions are linked to greater ambition and intelligence, though excess is harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of teleological/functionalist accounts of the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes refuses to talk about the purposes of the passions and resists functional/teleological explanations, an approach that made him congenial to authors like Spinoza.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodological stance undergirds Hobbes's materialist account (passions as motions) and his emphasis on naturalistic mechanics rather than purposes; later authors interpret or adopt aspects of this stance (e.g., Spinoza's expanded conatus and the maxim 'only an affect can overcome an affect').
